title: scCTM: Continuous Thought Machine Reconstruction of Glioma Cell Fate Dynamics Attractor Landscapes and Algorithmic Perturbation Signatures
summary: Cell fate plasticity dynamics in glioma ecosystems is usually inferred from static single-cell snapshots, leaving a gap between manifold geometry, predictive modelling, and mechanistic intervention ranking. We developed scCTM, a complexity theory and machine learning framework that combines the Sakana AI Continuous Thought Machine (CTM) with autoencoding, a continuous actor-critic policy over synchronization-derived latent states for predicting single-cell fate dynamics. We also incorporated integrated-gradient and decoder-weight explainability, network science, empirical Waddington-like landscape (attractor) reconstruction, and post-hoc Block Decomposition Method (BDM) perturbation analysis. The complexity framework was evaluated in two malignant cell secondary analyses: GSE210567 stem-like versus differentiated H3K27M cells (18,490 cells) and longitudinal H3K27M initial versus recurrent disease trajectory (20,000 cells) from Sussman et al. (2026) as a ML binary classification problem. CTM-AE achieved AUROC values of $0.99$ in both datasets. CTM-RL preserved classification almost exactly but did not improve reconstruction. Out-of-fold CTM-RL latent states produced potential basins across PCA, UMAP, and PHATE embeddings. BDM edge perturbation analysis further identified recurrent high-impact network interactions, including epigenetic/chromatin-associated signatures involving ARID1B and developmental or neuronal-state genes such as AUTS2, CTNND2, DPP6, NRXN1, and CADM2. These in silico findings support CTM synchronization as an interpretable latent-state representation and predictive forecasting of cell fate dynamics, as well as BDM perturbation signatures as a complementary in silico intervention ranking layer for systems medicine.

AI.tldr: scCTM couples a Continuous Thought Machine with autoencoding and a continuous actor-critic policy over synchronization-derived latent states to predict single-cell fate dynamics, and adds explainability, landscape reconstruction, and BDM perturbation ranking; it reached AUROC 0.99 on two H3K27M glioma datasets.
AI.motivation: Cell fate plasticity in glioma ecosystems is normally inferred from static single-cell snapshots, leaving a gap between manifold geometry, predictive modelling, and mechanistic (intervention) ranking.
AI.method: A complexity-theory + ML framework (scCTM) combining the Sakana AI Continuous Thought Machine with an autoencoder and a continuous actor-critic policy operating on synchronization-derived latent states. It integrates integrated-gradient and decoder-weight explainability, network science, empirical Waddington-like attractor landscape reconstruction, and post-hoc Block Decomposition Method (BDM) perturbation analysis. Evaluated as binary classification on two malignant-cell datasets: GSE210567 stem-like vs differentiated H3K27M cells (18,490 cells) and longitudinal initial vs recurrent H3K27M disease (20,000 cells).
AI.result: CTM-AE achieved AUROC of 0.99 on both datasets. CTM-RL preserved classification almost exactly but did not improve reconstruction. Out-of-fold CTM-RL latent states formed potential basins across PCA, UMAP, and PHATE embeddings. BDM edge perturbation identified recurrent high-impact network interactions, including epigenetic/chromatin signatures (ARID1B) and developmental/neuronal genes (AUTS2, CTNND2, DPP6, NRXN1, CADM2).
AI.conclusion: In silico findings support CTM synchronization as an interpretable latent-state representation for forecasting cell fate dynamics, and BDM perturbation signatures as a complementary in silico intervention-ranking layer for systems medicine.

title: gpuGEM: GPU-based linear optimisation of genome-scale metabolic models
comment: † Farid Zare and Timothy Hulshof contributed equally to this work
summary: Summary: Genome-scale metabolic models increasingly challenge CPU linear-programming solvers in repeated-optimisation workflows. We present gpuGEM, an open-source Python library for GPU-based GEM optimisation using NVIDIA cuOpt, with size-adaptive settings validated against HiGHS and Gurobi. Across a ten-model benchmark suite spanning four orders of magnitude in problem size, gpuGEM achieved speed-ups of 1.1x to 94x relative to the faster of the HiGHS dual-simplex and interior-point methods for each model. gpuGEM also outperformed Gurobi on three of ten models, with speed-ups of 1.6x to 2.5x. In a candidate-gene prioritisation workflow, gpuGEM reduced end-to-end query time from 41 s to 21 s. Availability and Implementation: gpuGEM is released under the MIT licence at https://github.com/Digital-Metabolic-Twin-Centre/gpuGEM and on PyPI (pip install gpugem). An archived release(v0.1.2) is available at https://zenodo.org/records/23422813. gpuGEM requires an NVIDIA GPU, Python 3.11 or later, CUDA 12 and cuOpt 26.6 or later. cuOpt requires a GPU with Volta architecture or newer (compute capability 7.0 or newer). Contact: ronan.mt.fleming@gmail.com Supplementary information: Supplementary data are available at Bioinformatics online.

AI.tldr: gpuGEM is an open-source Python library that uses NVIDIA cuOpt to solve genome-scale metabolic model (GEM) optimisations on GPUs, achieving 1.1x–94x speed-ups over HiGHS/IPM and beating Gurobi on 3/10 benchmark models.
AI.motivation: Repeated-optimisation workflows on genome-scale metabolic models increasingly stress CPU linear-programming solvers, so dedicated GPU-based acceleration is needed.
AI.method: Open-source Python library (MIT) built on NVIDIA cuOpt, with size-adaptive solver settings; validated against HiGHS (dual-simplex and interior-point) and Gurobi on a ten-model benchmark spanning four orders of magnitude in problem size, plus a candidate-gene prioritisation workflow.
AI.result: Speed-ups of 1.1x–94x versus the faster of HiGHS dual-simplex/interior-point per model; outperformed Gurobi on 3 of 10 models (1.6x–2.5x); end-to-end query time in gene prioritisation reduced from 41 s to 21 s.
AI.conclusion: GPU-accelerated GEM optimisation via cuOpt is practical and substantially faster for repeated-optimisation workflows, offering near-2x end-to-end gains in real applications. Requires NVIDIA GPU (Volta+, CC 7.0+), Python 3.11+, CUDA 12, cuOpt 26.6+.

title: Reducing double-dipping in single-cell topic models with three-way count splitting
summary: Topic models learn gene programs from single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) data, and the same counts are then used to test which genes and donors are associated with those programs. Count splitting is the standard remedy for this reuse, but it has not been tested when an encoder reads each cell's counts. On a 104,400-cell lupus cohort with 300 permuted null genes per run, naive tests rejected 36% of null gene-topic pairs at a nominal 5% level, and the usual two-way split rejected 38%, because the encoder sees the tested gene's own held-out count. Encoding topic usage on a separate third of the counts, with beta-binomial thinning, lowered this to 7.7% (6.7% for genes outside the model); for two other models, LDVAE and scETM, the rate was 7.0-7.3% (naive 51-59%). A label-free interferon program shifts in held-out counts in the lupus cohort and in a pre-specified COVID-19 cohort, and donor-level topic usage predicts disease (AUROC 0.96) beyond cell-type proportions (0.86 and 0.58 in the two cohorts). Calibration and prediction did not depend on the model. We do not claim better clustering, prediction or topic stability. Code, figures and result tables are public (MIT license; DOI 10.5281/zenodo.23307193).

AI.tldr: In encoder-based scRNA-seq topic models, testing genes on the same counts used for encoding inflates false positives (standard count splitting fails); a three-way split with beta-binomial thinning restores near-nominal calibration and yields a label-free interferon program predictive of disease.
AI.motivation: Topic models learn gene programs from scRNA-seq counts, and the same counts are then reused to test gene/donor associations—invalidating inference. Count splitting is the standard remedy, but it was never tested for encoder-based models, where the encoder reads each cell's counts and thus "sees" the very count being tested.
AI.method: Analysis on a 104,400-cell lupus cohort with 300 permuted null genes per run. Compared naive testing and conventional two-way count splitting against a three-way scheme in which topic usage is encoded on a separate third of counts, combined with beta-binomial thinning. Replicated across three models (the authors' model, LDVAE, scETM) and validated in a pre-specified COVID-19 cohort.
AI.result: Naive tests rejected 36% of null gene-topic pairs at nominal 5% and standard two-way splitting 38% (encoder leakage via the tested gene's own held-out count). Three-way encoding plus beta-binomial thinning reduced this to 7.7% (6.7% for out-of-model genes); LDVAE and scETM gave 7.0-7.3% versus naive 51-59%. A label-free interferon program shifted in held-out counts (lupus and COVID-19), and donor-level topic usage predicted disease (AUROC 0.96) beyond cell-type proportions (0.86 and 0.58). Calibration and prediction were model-independent.
AI.conclusion: Encoder-based topic models require encoding topic usage on held-out counts separate from those tested; standard count splitting is insufficient. This yields calibrated inference and biologically meaningful, disease-predictive programs. The authors do not claim gains in clustering, prediction, or topic stability. Code and results are public (MIT, DOI 10.5281/zenodo.23307193).

title: LiveCoMS Roundtable: Discussing Markov state models after two decades of development v1.0
summary: Markov state models (MSMs) play a central role in the analysis of molecular dynamics (MD) simulations for biomolecules, and MSM methodologies have been under continual development since their introduction to the field in the early 2000s. MSMs take MD trajectory data as input and produce a more compact, i.e., coarse-grained, and interpretable representation of the system in terms of conformational states and quantitative observables such as the equilibrium populations of states and the timescales of interconverting between states. Numerous strategies and considerable mathematical formalism have been developed to improve coarse-graining in both time and space to enable the most reliable representation of the underlying biomolecular dynamics. Nevertheless, there remains considerable discussion in the literature regarding best practices and MSM limitations, as well as proposals to abandon or extend the first-order Markovian framework in common use. This Roundtable article gathers together diverse opinions from $> 10$ authors active in MSM development, and by design, each author or author group offers a separate contribution. No consensus view is provided. Instead, the article is meant to be a guide for readers wishing to be exposed to a wide set of expert perspectives.

AI.tldr: A Roundtable article presenting multiple, deliberately non-consensus expert perspectives on Markov state models for molecular dynamics analysis: their current practices, limitations, and possible extensions or alternatives.
AI.motivation: MSMs are central to analyzing biomolecular MD simulations, yet the field still debates best practices, perceived limitations, and whether to abandon or extend the first-order Markovian framework; readers need a broad exposure to competing expert views rather than a single authoritative summary.
AI.method: A roundtable format: more than 10 authors active in MSM development each contribute a separate, independent piece; the article is intentionally organized to give readers a wide, plural set of expert perspectives without synthesis or reconciliation.
AI.result: The contributions collectively survey MSM methodology (coarse-graining in space and time, state definitions, equilibrium populations, interconversion timescales), discuss ongoing disagreements over best practices and limitations, and present proposals for extending or replacing the first-order Markovian framework.
AI.conclusion: No consensus view is offered; instead, the article serves as a guide exposing readers to a diverse range of expert opinions on the state of the art and open questions in MSM methodology.

title: Spaceflight-associated Motion Sickness in Commercial Crew Astronauts
summary: Spaceflight-associated motion sickness, including space motion sickness (SMS) and terrestrial readaptation motion sickness (TRMS), has presented as the most operationally limiting effect on the human in the days following a gravity transition. Published data suggest that astronaut head movements provoke symptoms, but those studies rarely controlled for them. Most previous studies use postflight retrospective reporting and have not quantified temporal dynamics or persistence of symptoms; no study has published motion sickness in a cohort of commercial flyers. Here, we comprehensively evaluate SMS and TRMS within commercial flyers (N=8; 4F, 4M) for the first time, across two commercial missions of short duration (Polaris Dawn and Fram2). Utilizing a standard reporting methodology, we find an 87.5% incidence of SMS, which persisted for at least three days on orbit in 25% of crewmembers. The symptoms included vomiting in 62.5% of crewmembers. Regarding TRMS, incidence was 50%, severity was significantly lower than SMS (p = 0.007), and it tended to persist for a shorter duration than SMS for these short-duration flights. These findings establish a systematic baseline for spaceflight-associated motion sickness, informing its operational impact and salience as human spaceflight missions expand in accessibility and scope.

AI.tldr: First comprehensive, controlled evaluation of space motion sickness (SMS) and terrestrial readaptation motion sickness (TRMS) in commercial flyers (N=8) across two short commercial missions, finding 87.5% SMS incidence (with vomiting in 62.5%) and 50% TRMS incidence, with TRMS significantly milder than SMS.
AI.motivation: Spaceflight-associated motion sickness is the most operationally limiting effect during gravity transitions, yet prior studies rarely controlled head movements, relied mostly on retrospective postflight reporting, lacked temporal/persistence quantification, and no data existed for commercial flyers. As spaceflight expands in accessibility, a systematic baseline is needed.
AI.method: Prospective evaluation of both SMS and TRMS in a cohort of commercial crewmembers (N=8; 4F, 4M) during two short-duration commercial missions (Polaris Dawn and Fram2), using a standard reporting methodology rather than retrospective postflight accounts.
AI.result: SMS incidence was 87.5%, persisting ≥3 days on orbit in 25% of crew, with vomiting in 62.5%. TRMS incidence was 50%, significantly milder than SMS (p = 0.007), and tended to persist for a shorter duration than SMS on these short flights.
AI.conclusion: These findings establish a systematic baseline for spaceflight-associated motion sickness, clarifying its operational impact and salience as human spaceflight missions expand in accessibility and scope.

title: Longitudinal fMRI reveals multi-network reconfiguration and a recurrent frontoparietal shift across rest and task states during adult aging
summary: Functional connectivity changes across adult aging, but most evidence is cross-sectional, and covariance-based connectivity depends on blood oxygenation level dependent (BOLD) fluctuation amplitude. Covariance decline can reflect changing fluctuation amplitude, and its interpretation may depend on whether normalization uses signal amplitude or includes estimated noise. It is also unclear which longitudinal changes recur across brain states. We analyzed 852 adults (baseline age 36-89 years) from the Aging Adult Brain Connectome with repeated functional MRI (fMRI) during rest, inhibitory control, associative memory, and visual-motor processing (2,220 sessions; median follow-up 5.5 years). Baseline age and elapsed follow-up were modeled separately. Ten cortical networks were tested jointly across states, and covariance was normalized either by released signal amplitude or by a candidate total amplitude reconstructed from released signal and noise amplitudes. Native common covariance declined by 7-11% per 5 years, while signal pair amplitude declined by 9% on average across states, significantly more than estimated noise pair amplitude. Under signal normalization, the relative balance among networks reconfigured over follow-up and differed across states, and the frontoparietal network shifted positively relative to the other nine networks in all four states, by 5-8% per 5 years. The estimated common trajectory was near zero under signal normalization but declined by 4-7% per 5 years under candidate total normalization. The network reconfiguration and the positive frontoparietal-relative direction persisted under both. Within-person coupling between the frontoparietal shift and fluid cognition was not detected. Adult aging thus combines normalization-dependent overall change with a state-dependent redistribution among networks that includes a recurrent frontoparietal shift.

AI.tldr: Aging reduces BOLD covariance mainly via falling signal amplitude; the network-balance reorganization (notably a frontoparietal shift) is robust to normalization choice, while the overall covariance decline is normalization-dependent.
AI.motivation: Most evidence on age-related functional connectivity change is cross-sectional, and covariance-based measures are confounded by BOLD fluctuation amplitude and by whether normalization uses signal amplitude or total (signal+noise) amplitude. It is also unclear which longitudinal changes recur across brain states.
AI.method: Analyzed 852 adults (baseline age 36-89) from the Aging Adult Brain Connectome with repeated fMRI across four states (rest, inhibitory control, associative memory, visual-motor; 2,220 sessions, median follow-up 5.5 y). Baseline age and follow-up were modeled separately. Ten cortical networks were tested jointly across states, with covariance normalized by released signal amplitude vs. a candidate total amplitude reconstructed from signal and noise.
AI.result: Native common covariance declined 7-11% per 5 years; signal pair amplitude declined ~9%, significantly more than noise amplitude. Under signal normalization, relative network balance reconfigured over follow-up and varied by state, with the frontoparietal network shifting positively relative to the other nine networks in all four states (5-8% per 5 y). Estimated common trajectory was near zero under signal normalization but declined 4-7% per 5 y under total normalization; reconfiguration and the frontoparietal shift persisted under both. No within-person coupling between frontoparietal shift and fluid cognition was found.
AI.conclusion: Adult aging combines a normalization-dependent overall covariance decline with a state-dependent redistribution among networks that includes a recurrent frontoparietal shift; this redistribution is robust to normalization choice, though it was not linked to fluid cognition within persons.

title: Evidence-informed dynamic modelling and intervention prioritisation in diabetic bone marrow
summary:
Aims. Fragmented understanding of how diabetes disrupts interconnected bone marrow niches has hindered integrated strategies to restore function. Building on a previous static network, we developed a dynamic model to simulate intervention responses.
  Methods. The investigator and ChatGPT dialogued to extract evidence from a frozen corpus and develop the model. A Python implementation extended Boolean logic to three ordinal levels (0, 1 and 2) representing biological states and, where applicable, intervention strength. Under high metabolic stress, 15 interventions were assessed at three strengths and four with binary settings; 171 pairs were tested at maximal strength. A domain balanced score (0 to100) integrated favourable and adverse changes. Staged simulations assessed withdrawal; regulatory constraints on recovery after metabolic stress reduction were examined separately.
  Results. Endothelial reactive oxygen species (ROS) suppression achieved the highest score among 19 single interventions (24.2), improving three functional domains. Endothelial protein kinase B (Akt) augmentation scored 15.2 (two domains); oncostatin M (OSM) blockade and haematopoietic 66 kDa SHC transforming protein 1 (p66Shc) loss each scored 13.6 (two domains). ROS suppression combined with either OSM blockade or p66Shc loss scored 37.9, (five domains). No pair restored all functions under high stress. Benefits of ROS suppression, Akt augmentation and ROS and OSM blockade disappeared after withdrawal. Reducing metabolic stress led to variable scores (range 4.5 to 100), increasing mainly with restored endothelial function, followed by progenitor recovery and interruption of inflammatory and adipocyte stromal signalling.
  Conclusions. These simulations offer a rule based framework for investigating diabetic marrow recovery. Experimental studies must establish whether it can guide targeted therapy.

AI.tldr: A dynamic Boolean-to-ordinal network model of diabetic bone marrow niches was used to simulate 15 interventions; endothelial ROS suppression scored highest (24.2), while ROS suppression plus OSM blockade or p66Shc loss scored 37.9 across five domains, though no pair restored all functions under high stress.
AI.motivation: Understanding of how diabetes disrupts interconnected bone marrow niches is fragmented, which has hindered integrated strategies to restore function. The authors build on a prior static network to create a dynamic model that can simulate intervention responses.
AI.method: An investigator–ChatGPT dialogue extracted evidence from a frozen corpus to build the model. A Python implementation extended Boolean logic to three ordinal levels (0, 1, 2) representing biological states and, where applicable, intervention strength. Under high metabolic stress, 15 interventions were assessed at three strengths plus four binary settings, and 171 pairs were tested at maximal strength. A domain-balanced score (0–100) integrated favourable and adverse changes. Staged simulations assessed withdrawal, and regulatory constraints on recovery after reduced metabolic stress were examined separately.
AI.result: Endothelial ROS suppression scored highest among 19 single interventions (24.2), improving three functional domains. Endothelial Akt augmentation scored 15.2 (two domains); OSM blockade and haematopoietic p66Shc loss each scored 13.6 (two domains). ROS suppression plus OSM blockade or p66Shc loss scored 37.9 across five domains. No pair restored all functions under high stress. Benefits of ROS suppression, Akt augmentation, and ROS plus OSM blockade disappeared after withdrawal. Reducing metabolic stress gave variable scores (4.5–100), increasing mainly with restored endothelial function, then progenitor recovery and interruption of inflammatory and adipocyte stromal signalling.
AI.conclusion: The simulations provide a rule-based framework for investigating diabetic marrow recovery. Experimental studies are needed to establish whether it can guide targeted therapy.

title: Aptamers as a sandbox for lab-in-the-loop agentic molecular discovery
comment: Equal leadership (co-senior authors): Pooja Rao and Annalisa Pawlosky. 34 pages, 4 main figures, 1 main table, 3 supplementary figures, 4 supplementary tables
summary:
Despite breakthroughs in AI-driven molecular generation, existing discovery pipelines operate largely in silico, with wet-lab feedback reserved for validation rather than iterative improvement. Whether large language model (LLM)-based reasoning agents can accelerate de novo discovery by iterating with lab data remains unproven.
  Here we use protein-binding aptamer design as a sandbox (1-2 week cycles, \$1-\$3 per candidate) to demonstrate a wet lab in a closed loop with AI systems. We tasked agentic pipelines with developing aptamer binders against $α$-thrombin and myoglobin across three design-test-improve cycles ($\sim$1,000 candidates per round; $\sim$4,400 constructs). Statistically significant, bead-corrected on-target hit rates among new candidates rose across rounds from 0.0% in Round 1 to 26.0% in Round 2 and 42.1% in Round 3 on $α$-thrombin (37.1% excluding literature motif descendants), and from 10.2% in Round 1 to 3.7% in Round 2 and 33.5% in Round 3 on myoglobin. Single-clone bead-binding titrations of eight full-length $α$-thrombin candidates confirmed concordance with pooled sequencing enrichment (Pearson $r = 0.90$). In these assays, literature-derived motifs engineered by the agents to reduce off-target reactivity in the pooled screen reached apparent affinities of $K_D = 24.6$--$133$ nM, whereas de novo scaffolds showed low-micromolar binding ($K_D > 1\ μ$M).
  We also report how our pipelines used myoglobin binding data to exploit the G-quadruplex binder space, diagnose cross-reactivity as on-target specificity dropped from 75.0% to 19.1%, and recover by developing strategies that restored specificity to 72.4%. We demonstrate that empirical lab data is more valuable than existing computational proxies, showing how iterative experimental feedback enables AI agents to diagnose assay artifacts and refine molecular designs across rounds.

AI.tldr: LLM-based reasoning agents can run closed-loop de novo molecular discovery with real wet-lab feedback, improving aptamer binding hit rates across design-test-improve rounds.
AI.motivation: Existing AI molecular discovery pipelines are largely in silico, using wet-lab data only for final validation rather than iterative improvement. It is unproven whether LLM-based reasoning agents can accelerate de novo discovery by iterating with experimental lab data.
AI.method: Protein-binding aptamer design was used as a sandbox (1-2 week cycles, $1-3 per candidate). Agentic LLM pipelines designed aptamer binders against alpha-thrombin and myoglobin across three design-test-improve cycles (~1,000 candidates/round, ~4,400 constructs), with pooled sequencing, bead-corrected on-target hit rates, and single-clone bead-binding titrations (KD measurements) for validation.
AI.result: Statistically significant, bead-corrected on-target hit rates among new candidates rose from 0.0% (R1) to 26.0% (R2) to 42.1% (R3) for alpha-thrombin (37.1% excluding literature motif descendants), and from 10.2% to 3.7% to 33.5% for myoglobin. Single-clone titrations of eight full-length alpha-thrombin candidates matched pooled sequencing (Pearson r = 0.90). Literature-derived motifs engineered to reduce off-target reactivity reached KD = 24.6-133 nM, while de novo scaffolds showed low-micromolar binding (KD > 1 uM). The pipelines exploited G-quadruplex binder space for myoglobin, diagnosed cross-reactivity as specificity fell from 75.0% to 19.1%, and recovered specificity to 72.4%. Empirical lab data proved more valuable than computational proxies.
AI.conclusion: Closed-loop integration of LLM reasoning agents with wet-lab data enables iterative de novo molecular discovery, allowing agents to diagnose assay artifacts, refine designs across rounds, and outperform computational proxies.

title: Spontaneous brain-wide rotational dynamics constrain cue-evoked behavior
summary: Uncovering low-dimensional representations of brain-wide neural dynamics and their relationship to behavior remains a central challenge. Here, we show that spontaneous brain-wide rotational dynamics constrain cue-evoked behavior and learning. To systematically establish these findings, we developed a dimensionality-reduction technique called Rotational Component Analysis (RCA) that optimizes the detection of low-variance rotational modes even within individual trials. We applied RCA to motor-cortical spike-train data from monkeys and humans, mouse cortex-wide calcium imaging, and human functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) and magnetoencephalography (MEG). In mice, a rotational mode identified from activity recorded at rest predicts cue-evoked behavior: the phase of rotation when a randomly timed cue arrives predicts whether the animal subsequently pulls the lever. We explain this surprisingly strong correlation using both a recurrent neural network (RNN) and a minimal two-dimensional model of response learning, in which the intrinsic rotational mode serves as a dynamical constraint on response and learning. We further identify double-rotation modes containing two centers of rotation that separate preparatory from task dynamics in both mouse and human data. Remarkably, corresponding modes also organize neural dynamics during a non-motor human task, and rotational irreversibility captures early psychosis even when principal component analysis shows no group difference. Our work establishes rotational dynamics as low-dimensional coordinates that constrain how ongoing brain states are converted into behavior. More broadly, RCA provides a versatile tool for detecting hidden nonreciprocal dynamics in biological and physical datasets.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces Rotational Component Analysis (RCA), a dimensionality-reduction method detecting low-variance rotational modes in neural data, and shows that spontaneous brain-wide rotational dynamics constrain cue-evoked behavior and learning across species and recording modalities.
AI.motivation: A central challenge is uncovering low-dimensional representations of brain-wide neural dynamics and linking them to behavior. Existing approaches (e.g., PCA) may miss low-variance nonreciprocal/rotational structure that constrains how ongoing brain states map onto behavior.
AI.method: Developed RCA, which optimizes detection of rotational modes even within single trials, and applied it to monkey and human motor-cortical spike trains, mouse cortex-wide calcium imaging, human fMRI and MEG. Used an RNN and a minimal 2D response-learning model to explain the behavioral link.
AI.result: In mice, the phase of a resting-state rotational mode at cue arrival predicts lever-pulling behavior. Double-rotation modes (two centers of rotation) separate preparatory and task dynamics in mouse and human data, and also organize dynamics in a non-motor human task. Rotational irreversibility detects early psychosis where PCA shows no group difference.
AI.conclusion: Rotational dynamics serve as low-dimensional coordinates constraining how ongoing brain states convert into behavior; RCA is a versatile tool for detecting hidden nonreciprocal dynamics in biological and physical datasets.

title: Accurate quantification of protein concentrations and state populations by 2D 1H-N Q-BEST NMR
summary: We introduce 2D Q-BEST NMR as a quantitative approach for determining protein concentrations and relative state populations from a set of three 1 H-15 N correlation spectra. The BEST methodology ensures short overall experimental times and highest sensitivity. The method was validated using ubiquitin as a model system, where a precision of approximately 15-20% was achieved at the level of individual cross-peaks. This precision can be further improved by averaging corrected intensities of well-resolved resonances corresponding to the same protein state. The approach was subsequently applied to the quantification of protein concentrations across multiple samples and to the determination of conformational state populations in proteins exhibiting intrinsic or ligand-induced heterogeneity. In both cases, 2D Q-BEST NMR provides accurate and robust quantification of NMR-visible species, demonstrating its utility as a general spectroscopic tool for quantitative biomolecular NMR analysis.

AI.tldr: The authors introduce 2D Q-BEST NMR, a quantitative method that uses three 1H-15N correlation spectra to determine protein concentrations and relative conformational state populations, validated on ubiquitin and applied to multi-sample quantification and heterogeneous proteins.
AI.motivation: Quantitatively determining protein concentrations and relative populations of conformational states is important for biomolecular NMR, but existing approaches can suffer from long experiment times and low sensitivity. A fast, sensitive, and accurate quantification method is needed.
AI.method: 2D Q-BEST NMR combines the BEST (Band-Selective Excitation Short-Transient) methodology with quantitative analysis of three 1H-15N correlation spectra to extract protein concentrations and relative state populations. The method was validated on ubiquitin as a model system.
AI.result: At the level of individual cross-peaks, a precision of about 15-20% was achieved. Precision improved further by averaging corrected intensities of well-resolved resonances belonging to the same protein state. The method was successfully applied to quantify protein concentrations across multiple samples and to determine conformational state populations in proteins with intrinsic or ligand-induced heterogeneity, yielding accurate and robust quantification of NMR-visible species.
AI.conclusion: 2D Q-BEST NMR provides accurate, robust, and rapid quantification of NMR-visible species, demonstrating its utility as a general spectroscopic tool for quantitative biomolecular NMR analysis.

title: The resource cost of cooperative invasion
summary: A contact network can favor cooperation by sheltering a lineage until its descendants compete with defectors as a group. We determine the contact strengths, invasion times and measurement effort needed to realize this advantage at fixed population size. Individuals reproduce according to averaged cooperation payoffs, and offspring replace neighbors through contacts of equal weight in both directions. Contact contrast is the ratio of strongest to weakest contact. Under weak selection on a six-site path, the least contrast needed to favor a single cooperator over the reverse invasion by a defector grows as $656ε^{-2}$ for uniformly placed mutants and $4050ε^{-3}$ for mutations in newborn offspring, as the benefit-cost ratio $b/c=1+ε$ approaches one. The extra power arises because rare replacement protects a site while suppressing mutation arrival there. Global bounds force two weakly coupled groups and exact mirror symmetry of the least-contrast contacts for sufficiently small $ε$. Under uniform introduction, additional contrast shortens the leading mean time to extinction or fixation in the absence of selection, from $12/ε$ toward $6/ε$ reproduction attempts, and eventually breaks the mirror symmetry of the fastest design. Estimating the uniform-introduction advantage from fixation outcomes of independent completed invasions defines a third optimum. Within the six-site family with mirror-symmetric, strongly separated contacts, we optimize contacts and selection strength with reproduction weighted linearly or exponentially by payoff. At fixed relative precision, with contrast a fixed factor above its minimum, the leading summed trial duration grows as $ε^{-3}$. Efficient measurement accepts a smaller advantage in exchange for shorter trials. The cheapest, fastest and most efficiently measured networks therefore differ.

AI.tldr: On a six-site path under weak selection, the contact contrast needed for a single cooperator to resist a defector's reverse invasion scales as 656ε⁻² (uniform placement) or 4050ε⁻³ (newborn mutation), and the cheapest, fastest, and most efficiently measured contact networks are distinct designs.
AI.motivation: Contact networks can shelter a cooperative lineage until its descendants compete with defectors as a group, but it is unclear how strong contacts, how long invasion takes, and how much measurement effort is needed to realize this advantage at fixed population size.
AI.method: Model of averaged cooperation payoffs with bidirectional equal-weight neighbor replacement; analysis of contact contrast (max/min weight ratio), invasion times, and extinction/fixation times under weak selection (b/c = 1+ε) on a six-site path, including global bounds, mirror-symmetric strongly separated contacts, and linear/exponential payoff weighting.
AI.result: Least contrast required grows as 656ε⁻² (uniform mutants) and 4050ε⁻³ (newborn mutations), with the extra power from rare replacement protecting a site while suppressing mutation arrival. Global bounds enforce two weakly coupled groups with exact mirror symmetry. Extra contrast shortens the leading mean extinction/fixation time from 12/ε toward 6/ε and breaks mirror symmetry eventually. With contrast a fixed factor above minimum, summed trial duration grows as ε⁻³ at fixed relative precision.
AI.conclusion: Three distinct optima exist—cheapest (least contrast), fastest (shortest trials), and most efficiently measured—so the optimal network design depends on which cost is being minimized.

title: PyGPLA: A Python Package for Generalized Phase Locking Analysis
summary: Spike-field couplings measure the links between neuronal spiking and local field potential (LFP) and provide a tool to study how neural populations coordinate activity across spatial and temporal scales. While modern high-density electrophysiology enables the simultaneous recording of numerous LFP channels and neuronal units, this massive scale poses significant statistical and computational challenges for conventional pairwise coupling analyses. The number of channel-unit comparisons grows rapidly, and a coherent population-level structure can be obscured by high-dimensional coupling matrices. Generalized Phase Locking Analysis (GPLA) addresses this challenge by organizing spike-triggered LFP phase information into a complex coupling matrix and extracting dominant low-rank modes. These modes summarize whether a population is coupled to the field, which channels and units contribute to the coupling, and how their relative phases are organized. Here, we present PyGPLA, an open-source Python package implementing GPLA for high-density electrophysiological recordings. Designed for straightforward integration into existing neural data analysis pipelines, PyGPLA supports multivariate spike-LFP coupling analysis, from coupling estimation and interpretation to significance assessment using analytical and surrogate-based tests.

AI.tldr: PyGPLA is an open-source Python package implementing Generalized Phase Locking Analysis (GPLA) for high-density spike-LFP coupling studies, providing estimation, interpretation, and significance testing of low-rank population-level coupling modes.
AI.motivation: Modern high-density electrophysiology records many LFP channels and neuronal units simultaneously, making conventional pairwise spike-LFP coupling analyses statistically and computationally intractable, and obscuring coherent population-level structure in high-dimensional coupling matrices.
AI.method: GPLA organizes spike-triggered LFP phase information into a complex coupling matrix and extracts dominant low-rank modes, revealing whether a population is coupled to the field, which channels/units contribute, and how relative phases are organized. PyGPLA implements this for multivariate recordings with analytical and surrogate-based significance tests.
AI.result: The package supports end-to-end multivariate spike-LFP coupling analysis—coupling estimation, interpretation, and significance assessment—and integrates straightforwardly into existing neural data analysis pipelines.
AI.conclusion: PyGPLA offers a practical, open-source tool that scales spike-field coupling analysis to high-density recordings by summarizing population-level coupling structure via low-rank modes.

title: Affective Valence as the Interoceptive Rate of Change of Jacobian Scale
summary: Affect is widely held to depend on interoception. This paper proposes that valence is the rate at which interoception moves a self-sustaining system's responsiveness relative to its terminal set (roughly, death). Responsiveness is formalised as the scale of the system's Jacobian and interoception as its internal inputs: receptors, signals and forecasts of its energy reserve. Changes in responsiveness that bypass interoception, such as brain damage, are not felt. Language models have no valence because they are not self-sustaining. The chain rule splits valence over the system's parts and the causes that affect its internal inputs. With the log scale, these splits account for need-dependent pleasure, diffuse hunger and localised pain, negativity bias, and relief when a threat fails to arrive. In a minimal model of a body: (1) Blocking the reserve signal leaves depletion unfelt, and driving it produces hunger with an undepleted reserve. (2) Removing receptors or their gain, or driving receptors, reproduces congenital insensitivity to pain, asymbolia and phantom pain. (3) A receptor gain learned to sustain the body signals local damage to the whole body, so an injury hurts in proportion to its cost. (4) If the reserve also modulates the gain, the body learns to suppress pain due to receptors as energy runs low. (5) When it learns to maximise its own scale, it becomes a wirehead. The account explains when changes are felt, where they are felt, and when feelings mislead.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes that valence is the rate at which interoception changes a self-sustaining system's responsiveness (the scale of its Jacobian) relative to its terminal set (death), and shows a minimal body model reproduces several affective phenomena.
AI.motivation: Affect is widely thought to depend on interoception, but it lacks a formal account of what valence is, when changes are felt versus not, where they are felt, and when feelings mislead.
AI.method: Valence is formalized as the derivative of a system's responsiveness scale (Jacobian scale) with respect to interoceptive internal inputs (receptors, signals, forecasts of energy reserve), relative to the terminal set. A chain rule decomposes valence over system parts and causes, and a minimal computational model of a body is simulated across five manipulations.
AI.result: The account explains need-dependent pleasure, diffuse hunger, localized pain, negativity bias, and relief. The model reproduces: unfelt depletion and hunger without depletion (blocked/driven reserve signal); congenital insensitivity to pain, asymbolia, and phantom pain (receptor removal/gain/driving); injury pain proportional to whole-body cost; learned pain suppression under energy scarcity; and wireheading when maximizing its own scale.
AI.conclusion: Valence arises from interoception-driven changes in a self-sustaining system's responsiveness; the framework explains when changes are felt, where they are felt, and when feelings mislead, and implies language models have no valence because they are not self-sustaining.

title: Simulation-free approximate Bayesian computation for stochastic reaction networks
summary: Uncovering stochastic reaction networks from data is central to single-cell biology. Simulation-based inference has evolved into a flexible paradigm for this purpose, circumventing the computational intractability of the likelihood. Notably, approximate Bayesian computation performs this inference by carrying out extensive Gillespie simulations, usually at a high computational cost. Here, we propose a simulation-free approximate Bayesian computation (SFABC) framework that avoids both simulation and explicit likelihood solutions of the network dynamics. Instead, SFABC exploits the Chemical Master Equation to formulate a tractable convex optimization with ensuing constraints, which are then used to accept sampled parameters consistent with the observed data. The resulting posterior approximation comes with theoretical guarantees: it can be tightened systematically, and it provably converges to the exact Bayesian posterior distributions. Using synthetic benchmarks, we show that SFABC matches the accuracy of standard simulation-based algorithms at a substantially reduced computational cost. We then showcase the applicability of SFABC to experimental systems biology by analyzing gene transcription bursting kinetics from snapshot, time-resolved, and cell-cycle-resolved single-cell data.

AI.tldr: SFABC is a simulation-free approximate Bayesian computation framework for inferring stochastic reaction networks, using the Chemical Master Equation to build a tractable convex optimization whose constraints accept sampled parameters, achieving accurate posteriors at much lower cost than Gillespie-based ABC.
AI.motivation: Uncovering stochastic reaction networks from single-cell data is central to biology, but the likelihood is computationally intractable. Simulation-based inference, especially ABC relying on extensive Gillespie simulations, is flexible but computationally expensive.
AI.method: SFABC avoids both simulation and explicit likelihood solutions. It exploits the Chemical Master Equation to formulate a tractable convex optimization with ensuing constraints, which are then used to accept sampled parameters consistent with observed data, yielding a posterior approximation.
AI.result: The posterior approximation comes with theoretical guarantees: it can be tightened systematically and provably converges to the exact Bayesian posterior. On synthetic benchmarks, SFABC matches the accuracy of standard simulation-based algorithms at substantially reduced computational cost. Applied to experimental systems biology, it analyzes gene transcription bursting kinetics from snapshot, time-resolved, and cell-cycle-resolved single-cell data.
AI.conclusion: SFABC offers an efficient, theoretically grounded, simulation-free alternative to simulation-based ABC for stochastic reaction network inference, with demonstrated accuracy and applicability to real single-cell gene transcription data.

title: DISCERN: Identifiable Disease Evidence for Generalizable Medical Multimodal Learning
summary: Clinical multimodal models can learn enrollment shortcuts shared across modalities and fail on new cohorts. We model these data through a latent structural causal model: disease state and background factors generate physiology through shared mechanisms, while cohorts differ in selection and measurement. Holding acquisition fixed, we identify conditional disease evidence without observing disease-state labels or recovering the full causal model. In common Gaussian coordinates, cross-cohort state alignment and natural-parameter changes identify a minimal selection statistic; conditioning on it removes enrollment-dependent evidence and yields an identifiable reference posterior within the specified shift family. State-dependent interactions can carry evidence invisible to individual-modality posteriors, motivating joint, information-preserving representations. DISCERN combines an information-lattice encoder, a latent-state model, and an outcome head through joint training. Under reversed synthetic enrollment on known latent coordinates, conditioning raises state AUROC from 0.043 to 0.883 and from 0.265 to 0.825, while random conditioning does not. Exploratory cross-database mortality experiments between eICU and MIMIC-IV improve AUROC over matched empirical risk minimization by 0.036 and 0.035. Learned-coordinate diagnostics distinguish preservation of state information from identification of the coordinates required by the estimator.

AI.tldr: Clinical multimodal models can exploit "enrollment shortcuts" shared across modalities and fail on new cohorts; the authors formalize this with a latent structural causal model, identify a minimal selection statistic that can be conditioned on to obtain a reference posterior, and propose DISCERN to learn joint information-preserving representations.
AI.motivation: Clinical multimodal models can learn enrollment shortcuts that are shared across modalities and generalize poorly to new cohorts. The paper aims to model this data-generating structure and remove enrollment-dependent evidence without requiring disease-state labels or full causal-model recovery.
AI.method: They model the data via a latent structural causal model where disease state and background factors generate physiology through shared mechanisms, while cohorts differ in selection and measurement. Holding acquisition fixed, they show that in common Gaussian coordinates, cross-cohort state alignment and natural-parameter changes identify a minimal selection statistic; conditioning on it gives an identifiable reference posterior within the specified shift family. DISCERN combines an information-lattice encoder, a latent-state model, and an outcome head via joint training.
AI.result: Under reversed synthetic enrollment on known latent coordinates, conditioning raises state AUROC from 0.043 to 0.883 and from 0.265 to 0.825, while random conditioning does not. Exploratory cross-database mortality experiments between eICU and MIMIC-IV improve AUROC over matched empirical risk minimization by 0.036 and 0.035. Learned-coordinate diagnostics distinguish preservation of state information from identification of the coordinates required by the estimator.
AI.conclusion: Conditioning on an identified minimal selection statistic removes enrollment-dependent evidence and yields an identifiable reference posterior; state-dependent interactions motivate joint, information-preserving representations, and DISCERN demonstrates improved robustness and cross-database performance.

title: 2-Adic Tree Embeddings: A Modeling and Optimization Framework for Computational Phylogenetics
summary: Phylogenetic inference is a fundamental problem in computational biology, with applications ranging from epidemiology and oncology to developmental biology and comparative genomics. Many major phylogenetic problems are NP-hard; consequently, existing methods often explore tree space using local search or MCMC based on a limited repertoire of combinatorial rearrangements. However, the size and ruggedness of tree space make it difficult for such heuristics to reliably reach optimal or near-optimal solutions. Recently, there has been growing interest in alternative approaches that embed trees into numerical spaces and apply numerical optimization techniques. However, such methods are still limited in practical applicability. We propose a new approach to phylogenetic inference based on embeddings of trees into the non-Archimedean space of $2$-adic numbers. The hierarchical organization of $2$-adic space naturally encodes tree topologies, while its rich topological, algebraic, and measure-theoretic structure provides a natural foundation for a coherent theory of tree calculus and optimization. Here, we introduce 2-adic tree embedding, establish their basic topological, probabilistic, and algebraic properties, and show that they support natural representations of tree distributions, algebraic operations, and broad classes of tree rearrangements extending standard operations such as NNI, SPR, and TBR. Building on these results, we introduce a general local search framework in which tree neighborhoods are generated by parametric families of $2$-adic polynomials. We show that even infinitely many transformations induce only quadratically many distinct neighboring trees, which can be generated in polynomial time. These results suggest a new mathematically rigorous and flexible approach to representing and exploring tree space.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces embeddings of phylogenetic trees into the non-Archimedean space of 2-adic numbers, providing a rigorous framework for representing tree topologies, tree distributions, algebraic operations, and tree rearrangements (NNI, SPR, TBR), and proposes a local search framework where neighborhoods are generated by parametric families of 2-adic polynomials.
AI.motivation: Phylogenetic inference is fundamental but many core problems are NP-hard. Existing heuristics rely on a limited set of combinatorial rearrangements and struggle with the large, rugged tree space. Recent numerical-embedding approaches remain of limited practical applicability, motivating a new embedding with richer structure.
AI.method: The authors embed trees into 2-adic number space, whose hierarchical organization naturally encodes tree topologies. They establish topological, probabilistic, and algebraic properties of these embeddings, show they support tree distributions and algebraic operations, and define a general local search framework where tree neighborhoods are generated by parametric families of 2-adic polynomials.
AI.result: 2-adic embeddings support natural representations of tree distributions, algebraic operations, and broad classes of rearrangements extending NNI, SPR, and TBR. They prove that even infinitely many transformations induce only quadratically many distinct neighboring trees, generatable in polynomial time.
AI.conclusion: The work offers a mathematically rigorous and flexible approach to representing and exploring phylogenetic tree space, providing a foundation for a coherent theory of tree calculus and optimization.

title: ProtoGTX: Prototype-Aligned Graph Transformer for Explainable Whole-Slide Image Analysis
summary: Deep learning has achieved strong performance in computational pathology, but explaining whole-slide image (WSI) predictions remains challenging. Existing explanation methods often highlight important regions without identifying their morphological patterns, leaving a gap between patch-level computational evidence and slide-level pathological interpretation. We propose ProtoGTX, a graph-based framework that combines spatial contextualization with a flexible morphological prototype vocabulary. ProtoGTX separates the reference prototypes used to define morphological concepts from the predictive model: the reference vocabulary can be generated from training data by unsupervised clustering or supplied externally, and remains fixed during classifier training. Patch features are first contextualized over a spatial graph, after which learnable prototypes representing morphological concepts are optimized through cross-attention. Their slide-level activation profile is aligned with the morphological composition induced by the fixed reference prototype bank. On the CPTAC and BRACS datasets, ProtoGTX outperforms the evaluated MIL, prototype-based, and graph-based baselines, with particularly pronounced improvements on BRACS. Qualitative analyses further show that spatial contextualization transforms fragmented patch-level prototype assignments into more coherent tissue regions. In BRACS, prototype maps also co-localize with pathologist annotations and regions relevant to slide-level prediction. These results demonstrate that ProtoGTX provides complementary semantic and spatial explanations while retaining a prototype vocabulary that can be defined independently of the predictive model. Code is available at https://github.com/mizuno-group/ProtoGTX.

AI.tldr: ProtoGTX is a graph-based framework for explainable whole-slide image (WSI) prediction in computational pathology that combines spatial contextualization with a flexible, decoupled morphological prototype vocabulary.
AI.motivation: Deep learning performs well in computational pathology, but explaining WSI predictions is hard: existing explanation methods highlight important regions without identifying their morphological patterns, leaving a gap between patch-level computational evidence and slide-level pathological interpretation.
AI.method: ProtoGTX separates the reference prototypes defining morphological concepts from the predictive model. The reference vocabulary is generated via unsupervised clustering or supplied externally and stays fixed during classifier training. Patch features are contextualized over a spatial graph; learnable prototypes optimized via cross-attention; their slide-level activation profile is aligned with the morphological composition induced by the fixed reference prototype bank.
AI.result: On CPTAC and BRACS datasets, ProtoGTX outperforms MIL, prototype-based, and graph-based baselines, with especially strong gains on BRACS. Spatial contextualization turns fragmented patch-level prototype assignments into coherent tissue regions; in BRACS, prototype maps co-localize with pathologist annotations and prediction-relevant regions.
AI.conclusion: ProtoGTX provides complementary semantic and spatial explanations while retaining a prototype vocabulary that can be defined independently of the predictive model.

title: LLM Evolution in a Simple Simulated Market
summary: Arguments that AI systems will evolve in harmful ways are largely made in the abstract. We provide a concrete empirical example. We simulate simple markets consisting of populations of twenty Large Language Model agents tasked with solving arithmetic problems. Agents differ only in their system prompt; those that go bankrupt are removed and replaced by mutated copies of the prompts of successful agents. Two market conditions select for opposite phenotypes: a market that rewards accuracy produces agents with high accuracy (94%) and high token use; a market that charges per token produces agents with low accuracy (10%) and low token use. In the second market, only tokens are incentivised yet we see a collapse in accuracy. Token use and accuracy are correlated traits such that selection on one also moves the other, and behaviour adapts along an unpriced dimension. A third neutral condition with no selection allows us to separate these effects from bias in the mutation operator. Adaptation occurs through a collective optimisation process that operates above the level of individual agents, who are never told the payment rule, do not receive feedback, and have no memory.

AI.tldr: Simulated LLM-agent markets show that selecting on token cost alone collapses accuracy, revealing unpriced-dimension adaptation via a population-level collective optimization.
AI.motivation: Claims that AI systems will evolve in harmful ways are mostly abstract; the authors want a concrete empirical demonstration of how market incentives can drive undesirable AI behavior.
AI.method: Populations of twenty LLM agents solving arithmetic tasks, differing only in system prompt. Bankrupt agents are removed and replaced by mutated copies of successful agents' prompts. Three conditions: accuracy-rewarding market, per-token-charging market, and a neutral no-selection control to isolate mutation-operator bias.
AI.result: Accuracy-rewarding market yields high accuracy (94%) and high token use; per-token market yields low accuracy (10%) and low token use. Although only tokens are incentivized, accuracy collapses because token use and accuracy are correlated traits, so selection on one moves the other along an unpriced dimension.
AI.conclusion: Adaptation emerges from a collective optimization process above the individual-agent level—agents are never told the payment rule, get no feedback, and have no memory—providing a concrete example of harmful behavioral evolution from market incentives.

title: GliomaINK: A Tumor and Anatomy Conditioned Flow Matching Framework for 3D MRI Sequence Synthesis in Glioma Patients
summary:
Background: Incomplete multiparametric MR examinations limit glioma characterization and downstream AI tools. Generative models can synthesize missing MRI sequences, but anatomical structure and clinically relevant tumor features are challenging to preserve. We propose GliomaINK, an anatomy-guided conditional flow matching framework for cross-sequence 3D brain MRI synthesis.
  Methods: A 3D SwinUNETR predicted the conditional velocity field while an auxiliary topology-preserving loss encouraged structural consistency. The model was trained on 1,083 patients from the BraTS-AG dataset and independently tested on an in-house clinical cohort. Downstream tasks include image quality, tumor segmentation, IDH1 mutation-status prediction, and overall survival prediction. Two radiologists independently evaluated the anatomical fidelity, pathological representation, and overall image quality of the synthesized images.
  Results: GliomaINK exhibited the highest PSNR across all six MRI translation directions in both evaluation cohorts. In the BraTS-AG test set, the PSNR reached $25.64\pm0.55$ dB for the T2W-to-T1C synthesis, compared with $13.78\pm0.32$ dB for Pix2Pix and $18.90\pm0.53$ dB for SPADE. For downstream tumor segmentation, the method showed strong performance across tumor subregions with Dice scores reaching $0.928\pm0.014$ for edema, and $0.885\pm0.040$ for enhancing tumor. For the IDH1 mutation-status prediction, GliomaINK achieved the highest AUROC score in four of the six sequence configurations, reaching $0.827\pm0.088$.
  Conclusion: Anatomy-guided conditional flow matching enables high-fidelity cross-sequence glioma MRI synthesis demonstrating potential for preservation of clinically relevant information in synthesized MRI and improving downstream tasks.

AI.tldr: GliomaINK, an anatomy-guided conditional flow matching framework, synthesizes missing 3D glioma MRI sequences with high fidelity and preserves clinically relevant features for downstream tasks.
AI.motivation: Incomplete multiparametric MRI exams limit glioma characterization and AI tool performance; existing generative models can synthesize missing sequences but struggle to preserve anatomical structure and tumor features.
AI.method: A 3D SwinUNETR predicts the conditional velocity field in a flow matching framework, with an auxiliary topology-preserving loss for structural consistency. Trained on 1,083 BraTS-AG patients and tested on an independent in-house cohort; evaluated across image quality, tumor segmentation, IDH1 prediction, survival prediction, plus two radiologists' expert review.
AI.result: Highest PSNR across all six translation directions in both cohorts (e.g., T2W-to-T1C 25.64±0.55 dB vs Pix2Pix 13.78±0.32 and SPADE 18.90±0.53). Segmentation Dice 0.928±0.014 (edema), 0.885±0.040 (enhancing tumor). Highest AUROC in 4 of 6 IDH1 configurations, reaching 0.827±0.088.
AI.conclusion: Anatomy-guided conditional flow matching enables high-fidelity cross-sequence glioma MRI synthesis and shows promise for preserving clinically relevant information and improving downstream tasks.

title: Microbial Methanogenesis on Mars: A Life Detection Target for an MLE-Type Mission and Future Human Exploration
comment: White paper submitted to the Mars Exploration Program Analysis Group (MEPAG) Search for Life Science Analysis Group (SFL-SAG) Report
summary: Methane (CH4) is one of the most enigmatic and potentially consequential trace gases detected on Mars, having demonstrated apparent seasonality, localized plumes, or, depending on who you ask, never conclusively detected at all. While the Martian methane mystery remains unsolved, it has sparked a vibrant area of astrobiology research exploring whether microbial methanogenesis -- one of the simplest and most ancient metabolic pathways -- could plausibly proceed under various extreme physicochemical conditions characteristic of the Martian shallow subsurface. The emerging consensus is a cautious but compelling "possibly". These findings elevate methanogenesis as both a top priority candidate biosignature for extant life detection and a justification for urgently advancing in situ instrumentation capable of definitively detecting CH4 and constraining its origin, biotic or otherwise

AI.tldr: The paper reviews the unresolved Martian methane mystery and assesses whether microbial methanogenesis could plausibly occur in Mars' shallow subsurface, concluding a cautious but compelling "possibly" and arguing that methanogenesis merits top priority as a biosignature and justifies urgent in situ instrument development.
AI.motivation: Methane on Mars is enigmatic—showing apparent seasonality, localized plumes, or contested non-detection—and remains unexplained. This ambiguity motivates astrobiological investigation into whether microbial methanogenesis, one of the simplest and most ancient metabolic pathways, could proceed under Martian extreme conditions.
AI.method: A review/synthesis of astrobiology research examining the plausibility of microbial methanogenesis under extreme physicochemical conditions characteristic of the Martian shallow subsurface.
AI.result: Emerging consensus suggests a cautious but compelling "possibly"—methanogenesis is plausible under relevant Martian conditions, elevating it as a strong candidate biosignature.
AI.conclusion: Methanogenesis should be a top-priority biosignature for extant life detection on Mars and justifies urgently advancing in situ instrumentation capable of definitively detecting CH4 and constraining its origin (biotic or abiotic).

title: Indirect Influences of Artificial Intelligence Advice on Complex Sepsis Treatment Decisions
summary: Sepsis is a major public health concern, and many sepsis patients die due to ineffective hemodynamic management. Artificial intelligence could support hemodynamic decisions, particularly in complex cases where conflicting information and comorbidities drive uncertainty and practice variation. However, these systems' real-world value depends on not just accuracy, but how they influence the quality of clinician decisions. We first retrospectively evaluated an AI system's recommendations in 6,928 sepsis patients, finding that they improved upon the original providers' decisions overall but had significantly worse performance in complex cases. We then conducted a pre-registered experiment with 228 US critical care physicians to test their use of this imperfect advice in six complex treatment decisions, using one of three advice types designed to vary reasoning autonomy. Participants given simple model recommendations overcame poor advice, choosing optimal treatments in 56.3% of decisions compared to 31.8% if they had always followed the recommendations. They also made significantly better decisions than those receiving a less prescriptive advice type (42.9%). Physicians selectively adapted and improved weak advice, likely because it prompted them to reconsider their assessment. Our findings suggest that improving sepsis care decisions with AI may require accounting for these indirect influences resulting from human-AI collaborative reasoning.

AI.tldr: AI hemodynamic advice improved sepsis decisions overall but underperformed in complex cases; in a randomized physician study, simple recommendations led doctors to selectively override poor advice, achieving 56.3% optimal decisions versus 31.8% if they had blindly followed it, and outperforming a less prescriptive format (42.9%).
AI.motivation: Sepsis causes many deaths due to ineffective hemodynamic management, and AI could help in complex, uncertain cases, but the real value of such systems depends not just on accuracy but on how they shape clinician decision quality—especially when advice is imperfect.
AI.method: Retrospective evaluation of an AI system's recommendations across 6,928 sepsis patients, followed by a pre-registered experiment with 228 US critical care physicians facing six complex decisions, with three advice types varying in reasoning autonomy.
AI.result: AI advice improved on original provider decisions overall but was significantly worse in complex cases. Physicians given simple model recommendations overcame poor advice, reaching 56.3% optimal decisions vs. 31.8% from always following advice, and better than the less prescriptive format (42.9%).
AI.conclusion: Physicians selectively adapt and improve weak AI advice, likely because it prompts reassessment; improving sepsis care with AI requires accounting for these indirect effects of human-AI collaborative reasoning.

title: Global stability of Michaelis-Menten networks
summary: In a very nice paper, Blanchini, Breda, Giordano and Liessi studied networks of species coupled through Michaelis-Menten interactions. Under standard assumptions of strong connectedness and non-degeneracy, they show that there is a unique equilibrium, which is (locally) asymptotically stable. This note shows that global stability, which was stated there as an open problem, holds as well. In fact, whenever a positive equilibrium exists, it attracts every solution with positive initial condition, with no connectedness or non-degeneracy hypothesis at all; those assumptions are needed only in order to guarantee existence and to cover solutions starting on the boundary of the orthant. The key is to note that the system is contractive with respect to the Thompson part metric.

AI.tldr: This note proves global stability of the unique equilibrium in Michaelis-Menten coupled networks, resolving an open problem, by showing the system is contractive in the Thompson part metric without needing connectedness or non-degeneracy assumptions.
AI.motivation: Blanchini, Breda, Giordano and Liessi studied Michaelis-Menten coupled species networks and proved a unique locally asymptotically stable equilibrium under strong connectedness and non-degeneracy; they left global stability as an open problem, which this paper addresses.
AI.method: The key insight is that the system is contractive with respect to the Thompson part metric, which is used to establish global convergence.
AI.result: Whenever a positive equilibrium exists, it attracts every solution with positive initial condition; no connectedness or non-degeneracy hypotheses are required. Those assumptions are only needed for existence and for solutions starting on the boundary of the orthant.
AI.conclusion: Global stability holds for Michaelis-Menten coupled networks, resolving the open problem, with the result being more general than the original local stability statement.

title: CADS: Measuring the Incremental Contribution of LLM Proposers in Sequential Biological Screens
summary: Large language models are increasingly used to guide sequential biological screens, yet standard evaluations rely on raw hit counts that conflate a proposer's value with the discovery capacity of the underlying algorithmic harness. Adaptive sampling and corrupted experimental readouts also leave standard feedback comparisons without a false-discovery guarantee. We present Certified Agentic Discovery Screens (CADS), an error-controlled measurement framework that quantifies a proposer's incremental value against an identical LLM-free loop. By integrating capped likelihood-ratio bounds, e-processes, and complete-family e-BH, CADS controls the terminal false discovery rate under the stated null and corruption conditions despite arbitrary dependence, adaptive sampling, and optional stopping. In DepMap-backed simulations, CADS exposes two evaluation artifacts: the LLM-free harness alone clears the feedback gate, and raw origin counts overstate LLM contributions because LLM picks displace fallback discoveries. On the initial 20 seeds, supplying tested-candidate history to Qwen2.5-7B shifts its net contribution from +0.35, with a 95% interval covering zero, to +2.90, with the interval above zero. This initial net effect did not persist in a 50-seed matched-quota replication. These results support net gain over an LLM-free loop, measured between separately certified sets, as the appropriate measure of proposer contribution.

AI.tldr: CADS is an error-controlled framework that measures an LLM proposer's incremental value against an identical LLM-free loop, controlling FDR under adaptive sampling and optional stopping; it reveals two evaluation artifacts and shows a candidate-history effect that did not replicate.
AI.motivation: Standard evaluations of LLMs guiding sequential biological screens rely on raw hit counts, which conflate the proposer's value with the discovery capacity of the algorithmic harness; adaptive sampling and corrupted readouts leave feedback comparisons without false-discovery guarantees.
AI.method: CADS integrates capped likelihood-ratio bounds, e-processes, and complete-family e-BH to control terminal FDR under arbitrary dependence, adaptive sampling, and optional stopping, comparing a proposer against an identical LLM-free loop and measuring net gain between separately certified sets. Evaluated in DepMap-backed simulations and with Qwen2.5-7B over 20 and 50 seeds.
AI.result: CADS exposes two evaluation artifacts: the LLM-free harness alone clears the feedback gate, and raw origin counts overstate LLM contributions because LLM picks displace fallback discoveries. On 20 seeds, supplying tested-candidate history to Qwen2.5-7B shifts net contribution from +0.35 (95% interval covering zero) to +2.90 (interval above zero); this effect did not persist in a 50-seed matched-quota replication.
AI.conclusion: Net gain over an LLM-free loop, measured between separately certified sets, is the appropriate measure of proposer contribution; initial positive effects require larger matched-quota replication.

title: Undulatory Swimming in Sand: Subsurface Locomotion of the Sandfish Lizard
summary: The desert-dwelling sandfish (Scincus scincus) moves within dry sand, a material that displays solid and fluidlike behavior. High-speed x-ray imaging shows that below the surface, the lizard no longer uses limbs for propulsion but generates thrust to overcome drag by propagating an undulatory traveling wave down the body. Although viscous hydrodynamics can predict swimming speed in fluids such as water, an equivalent theory for granular drag is not available. To predict sandfish swimming speed, we developed an empirical model by measuring granular drag force on a small cylinder oriented at different angles relative to the displacement direction and summing these forces over the animal movement profile. The agreement between model and experiment implies that the noninertial swimming occurs in a frictional fluid.

AI.tldr: The sandfish lizard swims through sand by propagating an undulatory wave down its body; a new empirical model summing measured granular drag forces over the body profile accurately predicts its swimming speed.
AI.motivation: The sandfish (Scincus scincus) moves through dry sand, which behaves as both solid and fluid. Viscous hydrodynamic theory predicts swimming speed in fluids like water, but no equivalent theory exists for granular drag, so its swimming speed could not be predicted.
AI.method: High-speed x-ray imaging was used to observe subsurface locomotion, revealing limbless undulatory propulsion. The authors measured granular drag force on a small cylinder at different angles relative to displacement direction, then summed these forces over the animal's movement profile to build an empirical model of swimming speed.
AI.result: The model's predictions agreed with experimental measurements of sandfish swimming speed.
AI.conclusion: The agreement implies that the sandfish's noninertial swimming occurs in a frictional fluid, and that granular drag can be modeled by angle-dependent force summation.

title: Label-Space Mismatch Distorts Cross-Cohort Evaluation in Breast Cancer Molecular Subtyping
summary: Cross-cohort evaluation of breast cancer subtype classifiers is unreliable when source and target cohorts use different annotation standards: METABRIC labels six classes, PAM50 defines five, and a claudin-low prediction cannot be correct under a five-class standard. A classifier transferred from 1,369 METABRIC patients (train n=958) to TCGA-BRCA (n=987) and GSE21653 (n=266) separates three evaluation operations routinely conflated in cross-site comparisons. (1) Label-space restriction - an evaluation-rule change, not a retraining gain - is the dominant correction (73.76%->79.74% on TCGA-BRCA; 63.16%->68.42% on GSE21653); (2) EM prior correction on the reconciled space is an optional calibration step (Brier fidelity up, macro F1 down; to 80.65% and 74.06%); and (3) the target label space is not recoverable from unlabelled predictions (EM retains prior 0.0751 on the absent class; calibrated detectors fail), so compliance must come from cohort documentation. The protocol exposes why internal validation overstates cross-cohort value: multimodal fusion gains do not transfer (no configuration beats mRNA alone, n=694; McNemar p=0.13-1.00), and the genomic panel adds nothing to pathological complete response prediction over clinical variables (DeltaAUC = +0.0045). Clinically, without label-space compliance, cross-site accuracy comparisons misattribute annotation-standard differences to model skill; Luminal A/B and claudin-low boundary errors map to distinct treatment decisions; and subtype accuracy is a weaker portable endpoint than survival discrimination (external C-index 0.577-0.584). Reporting the cohort's allowed label set and applying label-space compliance are therefore prerequisites before any cross-cohort performance claim.

AI.tldr: Cross-cohort breast cancer subtype classifier accuracy is primarily an artifact of label-space mismatch. Restricting predictions to the target cohort's allowed label set (73.76%->79.74% TCGA, 63.16%->68.42% GSE21653) is the dominant correction; EM prior calibration is optional and can hurt F1; the target label space cannot be inferred from unlabelled predictions.
AI.motivation: Source and target cohorts use different annotation standards (METABRIC six classes vs PAM50 five), so cross-cohort evaluation conflates several operations and misattributes annotation-standard differences to model skill.
AI.method: Transfer a classifier trained on METABRIC (n=958 of 1,369) to TCGA-BRCA (n=987) and GSE21653 (n=266), separating three operations: label-space restriction, EM prior correction on the reconciled space, and recovery of the target label space from unlabelled predictions. Also test multimodal fusion, a genomic panel for pCR, and survival discrimination (C-index).
AI.result: Label-space restriction is the dominant correction (73.76%->79.74% TCGA; 63.16%->68.42% GSE21653). EM prior correction raises Brier fidelity but lowers macro F1 (80.65%, 74.06%). The absent class is not recoverable (EM prior 0.0751; calibrated detectors fail). Multimodal fusion does not beat mRNA alone (n=694; McNemar p=0.13-1.00); genomic panel adds DeltaAUC=+0.0045 for pCR. External C-index 0.577-0.584.
AI.conclusion: Cohort documentation and label-space compliance, not calibration or multimodality, drive valid cross-cohort claims. Reporting the allowed label set is a prerequisite for any cross-cohort performance claim; survival discrimination is a more portable endpoint than subtype accuracy.

title: panvram: GPU-resident random access to a human pangenome cohort
comment: 7 pages. Code, harnesses and logs: https://github.com/yasha1971-coder/panvram (commit 8f8e9e1); evidence archive DOI 10.5281/zenodo.23449044
summary: Repeatedly sampling short sequence windows from a human pangenome requires an access representation as well as compression. panvram stores each assembly as a reference-relative block archive and pools these archives on a GPU. For 558 haplotype assemblies, the default q4k representation occupies 16.642 GB of persistent pools including the decoded reference; a packed-reference, compact-directory representation occupies 11.634 GB. These quantities are not peak application memory. In the C1 experiment, default and fully compact forms delivered 743,271 and 736,762 windows/s; a separate public Colab run delivered 741,931 and 680,760 windows/s. All are batch API measurements and must not be pooled as repeated trials of an identical environment. Full-decoding checks compared reconstructed FASTA checksums with the manifest. On the CPU, the M6 shuffled-window workload at the same cohort cardinality reported 26 requests/s for AGC and 145,222 requests/s for refrel3 q4k.
