This comparison concerns one-thread requests of 4 KiB on the recorded warm-cache workload, not all genome-access patterns. AGC provides the smaller incremental archive: 5.40 MB/assembly versus 13.04 MB/assembly for refrel3 q16k, with different exclusions; the size pair is not the same refrel3 configuration as the q4k timing pair. We derive an expected-work expression for fixed independent granules and distinguish it from an empirical median-latency predictor. Cohort-scale counter and DRAM measurements motivate a locality hypothesis, but do not establish a causal per-miss latency or independently reproduce a model-failure verdict. The window-cost verdict at N=558 is published with its harness and raw timings.

AI.tldr: panvram stores each haplotype assembly as a reference-relative block archive and pools them on a GPU to serve repeated sampling of short sequence windows from a 558-haplotype human pangenome, quantifying sizes, throughput, and a CPU baseline comparison.
AI.motivation: Repeatedly sampling short windows from a human pangenome needs both a suitable access representation and compression; the paper reports such a representation's footprint, throughput, and a controlled CPU comparison.
AI.method: Reference-relative block archives per assembly pooled on GPU, in default q4k and packed-reference compact-directory forms; window-throughput batch API measurements, full-decoding FASTA checksum validation against the manifest, and single-thread warm-cache 4 KiB CPU comparisons (AGC vs refrel3) on shuffled-window workloads; an expected-work expression for fixed independent granules.
AI.result: 16.642 GB default vs 11.634 GB compact persistent pools (not peak memory) for 558 haplotypes; 743,271/736,762 windows/s on C1 and 741,931/680,760 on Colab; CPU 26 req/s (AGC) vs 145,222 req/s (refrel3 q4k); AGC 5.40 vs refrel3 q16k 13.04 MB/assembly incremental archives.
AI.conclusion: The N=558 window-cost verdict is released with harness and raw timings, but the reported figures are non-interchangeable measurements: environment-specific batch runs, non-identical configurations, and locality evidence that does not establish per-miss causality.

title: Simulating Infant Senses with Age-Tuned Networks
comment: 21 pages, 7 figures, 2 tables. Code and website: https://github.com/pikulsomesh/developmental-world-models and https://pikulsomesh.github.io/developmental-world-models/
summary: What a newborn sees, hears and feels, and how this changes month by month, has been measured sense by sense, with different methods and in different units. We bring these measurements together for the first two years of life and ask whether small neural networks tuned to a given age can turn them into a quick, inspectable simulation of sensory perception. Each sense's immaturity is written as a fixed, age-indexed filter on the input, and a small prediction network learns behind it over the first year. The filters alone reproduce the order in which the senses mature, by construction. The networks add what filters cannot: in vision they extract far less than their input allows at early stages (at the newborn stage a toy's position cannot be read out, $R^2 = 0.00$, against 0.57 for a network trained directly on the same input), and a critical period and perceptual narrowing emerge without being built in; in hearing they track what their input allows. The same filters drive the Baby Senses Lab, a free website that shows a user's own images and sounds as a baby of a chosen age might sense them. It is a research and teaching tool, not a diagnostic test.

AI.tldr: The authors compile sense-by-sense measurements of infant perception across the first two years, encode each sense's immaturity as a fixed age-indexed input filter, and train small prediction networks behind these filters. The learned networks reproduce developmental phenomena (critical periods, perceptual narrowing in vision) not explicitly built in, and power a free web tool, Baby Senses Lab.
AI.motivation: Infant sensory development has been measured separately for each sense, with different methods and units, making an integrated, inspectable picture of how perception changes month by month difficult to obtain.
AI.method: Each sense's immaturity is represented as a fixed, age-indexed filter on the input; a small neural network learns prediction behind that filter over the first year. Age-tuned networks are then compared against networks trained directly on the same input, and the filters drive a public website displaying user images and sounds as a baby of a chosen age might sense them.
AI.result: The filters reproduce the known order of sensory maturation by construction. In vision, early networks extract far less than their input permits (newborn toy-position readout R² = 0.00 vs. 0.57 for a network trained directly on the same input), and a critical period and perceptual narrowing emerge without being built in; in hearing, performance tracks what the input allows.
AI.conclusion: Small age-tuned networks behind fixed developmental filters can produce a quick, inspectable simulation of infant sensory perception and generate developmental phenomena emergently. The resulting Baby Senses Lab is offered as a research and teaching tool, not a diagnostic test.

title: HyperTaxa: Multiscale Genome Representations for Generalized Microbial Taxonomic Inference
summary: Reliable microbial taxonomic inference is challenged by the rapid growth of newly sequenced organisms and incomplete reference coverage. While alignment- and database-driven tools remain essential for reference-backed identification, they are not designed for learned inference over species absent from genome-level training. We introduce HyperTaxa, a taxonomy-aligned representation learning framework for open-set microbial taxonomic inference. HyperTaxa encodes whole genomes as multiscale hyperspectral k-mer transition fields and aligns these representations to a taxonomy-derived semantic space using a two-stage Node2Vec-to-MDS procedure that combines local graph structure with global hierarchical distance preservation. The resulting space supports zero-shot inference over species excluded from genome-level training but represented in the taxonomy, generalized zero-shot inference over seen and unseen species, and cascaded genus-to-species prediction. Across benchmark and large-scale disjoint-species evaluations, HyperTaxa improves taxonomic prediction over pseudo-image and transformer-graph baselines, with the strongest gains at higher taxonomic ranks. Ablations further show that multiscale transition encoding and taxonomy-aware alignment are key contributors to generalization. These results position HyperTaxa as a complementary taxonomy-aware representation and candidate-generation framework for microbial identification under incomplete reference coverage and open-set uncertainty.

AI.tldr: HyperTaxa is a taxonomy-aligned representation learning framework that enables open-set and zero-shot microbial taxonomic inference by encoding whole genomes as multiscale hyperspectral k-mer transition fields aligned to a taxonomy-derived semantic space.
AI.motivation: Microbial taxonomic inference struggles with rapidly growing newly sequenced organisms and incomplete reference coverage. Existing alignment- and database-driven tools require reference backing and cannot perform learned inference over species absent from genome-level training.
AI.method: Genomes are encoded as multiscale hyperspectral k-mer transition fields, then aligned to a taxonomy-derived semantic space via a two-stage Node2Vec-to-MDS procedure combining local graph structure with global hierarchical distance preservation. This supports zero-shot, generalized zero-shot, and cascaded genus-to-species prediction.
AI.result: On benchmark and large-scale disjoint-species evaluations, HyperTaxa outperforms pseudo-image and transformer-graph baselines, with the largest gains at higher taxonomic ranks. Ablations show multiscale transition encoding and taxonomy-aware alignment drive generalization.
AI.conclusion: HyperTaxa serves as a complementary taxonomy-aware representation and candidate-generation framework for microbial identification under incomplete reference coverage and open-set uncertainty.

title: HP-GSBS: Accelerating greedy state boundary search with reusable interval statistics
comment: 9 pages, 5 figures; 10-page supplementary material included (19 pages total)
summary: Greedy State Boundary Search (GSBS) identifies transitions between relatively stable neural activity patterns, but repeated candidate evaluation makes large analyses expensive. HP-GSBS is an open-source Python package that reorganizes the search around reusable interval contributions and correlation statistics. Streaming candidate reduction and local refinement further reduce repeated work; CPU, PyTorch CUDA and Triton backends share sequential segmentation decisions. Across seven controlled workloads with two realizations each, median same-input speedups range from 154 to 1730 times. All 168 optimized executions reproduce original boundaries and selected state counts, with maximum absolute t-distance difference $1.88\times10^{-11}$. Four frozen EEG recordings provide complementary validation, including a complete input-to-segmentation application example. Batch processing, versioned result persistence and optional low-memory execution support recording collections and longer inputs. By removing redundant computation, HP-GSBS makes established neural-state segmentation faster while preserving its scientific outputs.

AI.tldr: HP-GSBS is an open-source Python package that speeds up Greedy State Boundary Search for neural-state segmentation by reusing interval contributions and correlation statistics, achieving 154–1730x median speedups while exactly reproducing original boundaries and state counts.
AI.motivation: Original GSBS identifies transitions between stable neural activity patterns, but repeated candidate evaluation makes large analyses computationally expensive. The work aims to remove redundant computation without altering scientific outputs.
AI.method: Reorganizes the search around reusable interval contributions and correlation statistics. Adds streaming candidate reduction and local refinement, with CPU, PyTorch CUDA and Triton backends sharing sequential segmentation decisions. Also includes batch processing, versioned result persistence and optional low-memory execution.
AI.result: Across seven controlled workloads with two realizations each, median same-input speedups range from 154x to 1730x. All 168 optimized executions reproduce original boundaries and selected state counts, with max absolute t-distance difference of 1.88e-11. Four frozen EEG recordings provide complementary validation, including a full input-to-segmentation example.
AI.conclusion: By eliminating redundant computation, HP-GSBS makes established neural-state segmentation substantially faster while preserving identical scientific outputs, supporting larger recordings and longer inputs.

title: Distributions of metric $n$-point invariants and applications to molecular evolution
summary: Datasets often arise as samples from a metric measure space whose geometry reflects the data-generating process. We introduce metric $n$-point invariants, defined as functions of the pairwise distances of $n$-point configurations, to study the geometry of such spaces. This provides a unified framework for existing concepts, such as the pairwise distance itself, the Gromov product, and Vietoris-Rips persistence diagrams. The distribution of a metric $n$-point invariant $F$ over random $n$-point configurations can be used to extract geometric information from the space and is obtained as the pushforward of Gromov's $n$-th curvature measure $μ_n$ along $F$. Our main result is an explicit bound for the expected $p$-Wasserstein distance between $μ_n$ and the empirical curvature measure $\hatμ_{n}$ of finitely many sampled $n$-point configurations, and carries over to the associated distributions of Lipschitz metric $n$-point invariants. From this we derive the sample size needed to achieve a prescribed accuracy and level of confidence in the approximation of the curvature measure. As an application, we use metric $n$-point invariants to study molecular evolution. We describe how site-wise nucleotide frequencies shape the corresponding distributions in Jukes-Cantor and Halpern-Bruno substitution models, and analyse five million SARS-CoV-2 genomes, revealing increasingly common failures of the four-point condition, constrained nucleotide accessibility consistent with the biased mutation spectrum, and rare cycles in persistent homology reflecting recurrent mutations across lineages. These findings demonstrate the potential of our sampling-based approach to the geometry of data as a scalable, phylogeny-free tool for detecting and quantifying evolutionary structure in large genomic datasets.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces metric n-point invariants as a unified framework for studying the geometry of metric measure spaces, proves a finite-sample bound on the Wasserstein distance between the true n-th curvature measure and its empirical version, and applies the framework to study molecular evolution in five million SARS-CoV-2 genomes.
AI.motivation: Datasets are samples from a metric measure space whose geometry reflects the data-generating process, so extracting geometric information from such spaces is desirable. Existing concepts (pairwise distance, Gromov product, Vietoris-Rips persistence diagrams) are fragmented, and large-scale genomic data call for scalable, phylogeny-free geometric tools.
AI.method: Define metric n-point invariants as functions of pairwise distances of n-point configurations. Show their distribution over random configurations equals the pushforward of Gromov's n-th curvature measure along the invariant. Prove an explicit bound on the expected p-Wasserstein distance between the curvature measure and its empirical counterpart from finitely many sampled configurations, extending to Lipschitz invariants, and derive required sample sizes.
AI.result: The bound yields sample-size guarantees for prescribed accuracy and confidence. Applying the method to ~5 million SARS-CoV-2 genomes reveals increasingly common failures of the four-point condition, constrained nucleotide accessibility consistent with a biased mutation spectrum, and rare cycles in persistent homology reflecting recurrent mutations; Jukes-Cantor and Halpern-Bruno models are analyzed for site-wise nucleotide frequencies.
AI.conclusion: Sampling-based metric n-point invariants offer a scalable, phylogeny-free tool for detecting and quantifying evolutionary structure in large genomic datasets, validated both theoretically and empirically.

title: Higher-Order Co-Infection on Hypergraphs
summary: People encounter infections through overlapping groups, such as households, classrooms, and workplaces. Understanding how these shared contacts affect the spread of multiple pathogens is critical to determining what information epidemic models need to retain. We introduce HyCo-SIS (Higher-order Co-infection SIS), a discrete-time SIS model on hypergraphs with explicit reinforcement between overlapping active groups and pairwise transmission. We investigate how this reinforcement affects infection dynamics and whether simplified representations of hypergraphs preserve the resulting behavior. We derive an exact representation of overlap reinforcement as target-dependent four-person interactions and determine when a symmetric representation is possible. Numerical experiments examine reinforcement strength, contact structure, and susceptibility to secondary infection, as well as calibrated pairwise approximations. Our results demonstrate that redistributing overlap weights can substantially change finite-time co-infection even when every individual's total overlap coefficient is preserved. We further derive an exact five-person calculation and demonstrate why equal mean infection pressure does not necessarily produce equal acquisition probabilities. These findings identify how the allocation of higher-order interactions can influence contagion dynamics beyond their aggregate strength. Beyond epidemiology, this work contributes to the statistical physics of spreading processes by examining how the arrangement of many-body interactions shapes collective dynamics, and what information is lost when those interactions are simplified.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces HyCo-SIS, a discrete-time SIS model on hypergraphs with explicit reinforcement between overlapping active groups and pairwise transmission, and shows that how higher-order overlap interactions are allocated—not just their aggregate strength—substantially shapes co-infection dynamics, information that simplified pairwise representations may lose.
AI.motivation: People encounter infections through overlapping social groups (households, classrooms, workplaces), and understanding how shared contacts affect the spread of multiple pathogens is critical to deciding what information epidemic models must retain.
AI.method: The authors formulate a discrete-time SIS model on hypergraphs with explicit reinforcement between overlapping active groups plus pairwise transmission. They derive an exact representation of overlap reinforcement as target-dependent four-person interactions, determine when a symmetric representation is possible, and run numerical experiments varying reinforcement strength, contact structure, and secondary-infection susceptibility, including calibrated pairwise approximations.
AI.result: Redistributing overlap weights can substantially change finite-time co-infection even when every individual's total overlap coefficient is preserved. An exact five-person calculation shows that equal mean infection pressure does not necessarily produce equal acquisition probabilities.
AI.conclusion: The allocation of higher-order interactions influences contagion dynamics beyond their aggregate strength. The work contributes to the statistical physics of spreading processes by examining how the arrangement of many-body interactions shapes collective dynamics and what information is lost when those interactions are simplified.

title: How Robust Are Prognostic Radiomic Features? Comparing Selection Techniques on Pooled Glioblastoma Cohorts
summary: Radiomic survival studies in glioblastoma report heterogeneous prognostic features, but how much of this stems from the methodology itself is rarely examined. We analysed the association of 463 radiomic, anatomical and clinical features from pre-treatment MRI with overall survival in 705 IDH-wildtype glioblastoma patients from three public cohorts, using three techniques: a log-rank test after median split, univariate Cox regression (both Benjamini-Hochberg corrected) and an XGBoost regressor interpreted with SHAP. The log-rank test selected 99 features, Cox regression 72 and SHAP its top 20; five were selected by all three: age, a peritumoural T2 texture feature, the number of connected peritumoural mask components and two image-level intensity maxima. The two survival tests shared 51 features, about half of the SHAP top 20 were also selected by either test, and where selections overlapped, effect directions agreed. Many selections were PyRadiomics diagnostic descriptors that are not restricted to tumour voxels. Analytical pipeline choices, including ranking method, pre-filtering and descriptor handling, can substantially influence which features appear prognostic.

AI.tldr: In 705 IDH-wildtype glioblastoma patients from three public cohorts, the authors compared three feature-selection methods (median-split log-rank, univariate Cox, SHAP on an XGBoost model) across 463 radiomic, anatomical and clinical features. Selection was highly method-dependent: only 5 features overlapped across all three approaches, and many selected features were non-tumour-restricted PyRadiomics diagnostics, indicating analytical pipeline choices strongly shape which features appear prognostic.
AI.motivation: Radiomic survival studies in glioblastoma report heterogeneous and poorly reproducible prognostic features, but the extent to which this heterogeneity arises from the analysis methodology itself rather than biology is rarely examined. The authors aim to quantify how analytical choices (ranking technique, pre-filtering, descriptor handling) drive which features are declared prognostic.
AI.method: Retrospective analysis of 463 radiomic, anatomical and clinical features from pre-treatment MRI in 705 IDH-wildtype glioblastoma patients pooled from three public cohorts. Survival association with overall survival was assessed using three techniques: (1) log-rank test after median split, (2) univariate Cox regression (both Benjamini-Hochberg corrected), and (3) an XGBoost regressor interpreted with SHAP. Feature selections and effect directions were then compared across methods.
AI.result: The log-rank test selected 99 features, Cox regression 72, and SHAP its top 20. Only five features were selected by all three: age, a peritumoural T2 texture feature, the number of connected peritumoural mask components, and two image-level intensity maxima. The two survival tests shared 51 features; roughly half of the SHAP top 20 were also selected by at least one survival test, and overlapping selections agreed in effect direction. Many selected features were PyRadiomics diagnostic descriptors not restricted to tumour voxels.
AI.conclusion: Prognostic feature sets in glioblastoma radiomics are strongly contingent on the analytical pipeline. Method choice (ranking approach, pre-filtering, descriptor handling) substantially influences which features appear prognostic, and the reliance on non-tumour-restricted diagnostic descriptors raises validity concerns. Greater methodological transparency and caution are needed when interpreting radiomic survival signatures.

title: Small Average Error, Wide Individual Error: General-Purpose LLMs Estimating Energy Intake from Meal Photos in a Feeding Trial
comment: 20 pages, 1 figure, 12 tables. Code, prompts, pre-registration and per-meal outputs: https://github.com/xtea/llm-intake-validation
summary: Photo-based estimation of food energy could ease dietary assessment, and general-purpose multimodal large language models (LLMs) make such estimates easy to obtain. Most evaluations use one photo taken before eating and compare with energy served, while dietary assessment needs energy eaten. We evaluated six models from two vendors (Claude Haiku, Sonnet and Opus 5.5; GPT-6 luna, 6.1 sol and 6 astra) on 802 meals from ACETADA, a controlled feeding trial with weighed intake, with the before photo only, before and after photos in separate calls (subtraction), or both photos in one request. Three results ran against intuition. Subtraction under-estimated intake for five of six models, because the models still report hundreds of kilocalories for a nearly empty tray. Scaling the before-only estimate by the average share eaten (0.87) matched much of the gain from the after photo; beyond that constant, the second photo lowered meal-level error by only 2.2 to 3.4 points, mainly in meals with food left. With one photo, two models had a near-zero intake bias only because they under-estimated the served energy and ignored uneaten food. In ablations, adding the after photo improved accuracy under both prompt formats for five models, while prompt effects varied across models. Over 148 feeding days, three models kept the 90% confidence interval of their mean error within a pre-set 10% margin, but no model reached the pre-set 30% limits of agreement. Protein was under-estimated by every model, most in protein-dense meals; repeated calls changed error by at most 1.4 points; a high reasoning effort helped only the smallest model (4.2 points) and changed the others by less than 1 point. A low average bias is not evidence of accurate individual intake estimation; such estimates should support, not replace, assessment by a dietitian.

AI.tldr: Six multimodal LLMs were tested on photo-based estimation of energy eaten across 802 meals from a controlled feeding trial; counterintuitively, subtracting an after-photo estimate from a before-photo estimate under-estimated intake in five of six models, and low average bias did not imply accurate per-meal estimates.
AI.motivation: Dietary assessment needs energy actually eaten, but most photo-based evaluations compare a single pre-meal photo against energy served, not intake. Cheap access to general-purpose multimodal LLMs makes rigorous testing of intake estimation necessary.
AI.method: Evaluated six models (Claude Haiku, Sonnet, Opus 5.5; GPT-6 luna, 6.1 sol, 6 astra) on 802 weighed meals from ACETADA, a controlled feeding trial. Three protocols: before photo only, before and after photos in separate calls (subtraction), and both photos in one request. Also ablations on prompt format, repeated calls, reasoning effort, nutrient-level (protein) estimates, and day-level calibration over 148 feeding days.
AI.result: Subtraction under-estimated intake for five of six models because models still reported hundreds of kcal for near-empty trays. Scaling the before-only estimate by mean share eaten (0.87) reproduced much of the after-photo gain; beyond that constant, the second photo reduced meal-level error by only 2.2-3.4 points. Two models showed near-zero intake bias only by under-estimating served energy and ignoring leftovers. Adding the after photo helped five models across prompt formats. Three models kept their day-level 90% CI within a 10% margin, but none reached the 30% limits of agreement. Protein was under-estimated by all models, most in protein-dense meals; repeated calls changed error ≤1.4 points; high reasoning effort helped only the smallest model (4.2 points).
AI.conclusion: Photo-based LLM estimates can have low average bias without being accurate at the individual-meal level, and adding a second photo yields modest, largely constant-factor gains. Such tools should support, not replace, dietitian assessment.

title: Bombadil: A Foundation Model for Plant Electrophysiology
summary:
Living plants, like animals, use electrical signals to carry information about their physiological state across their body, from roots to branches. These signals can be recorded, as they are in animals, from a pair of differential extracellular electrodes inserted into signal-conducting tissue. While machine-learning models have been trained to predict specific plant stress states from these signals, each of these models has been trained for only a single task and none have been designed to transfer across tasks, species, or environments. These approaches do not allow easy scaling across the wide range of species and environments that are relevant to agriculture, forestry, and horticulture for both commercial and consumer plant care.
  Here we present Bombadil, a foundation model for plant electrophysiology, pretrained without labels on over 4 million hours of electrical signals recorded from 100 plant species in ten distinct environments, including laboratories, greenhouses, commercial orchards, and natural forests. In this way, Bombadil is able to learn the fundamental features of plant electrical signals across a wide array of species and environments. Then, from those same electrical signals, Bombadil tracks changes in seven physiological indicators of plant stress, even among species and stressors with no labels in training.

AI.tldr: Bombadil is a label-free foundation model for plant electrophysiology, pretrained on 4M+ hours of electrical signals from 100 species across 10 environments, and it tracks seven physiological stress indicators, generalizing to unseen species and stressors.
AI.motivation: Plants use electrical signals to carry physiological information across the body, which can be recorded with extracellular electrodes. However, existing machine-learning models are trained for single tasks and cannot transfer across tasks, species, or environments, limiting scalability for agriculture, forestry, and horticulture applications.
AI.method: The authors build Bombadil, a foundation model pretrained without labels on over 4 million hours of electrical signals from 100 plant species in ten environments (laboratories, greenhouses, commercial orchards, natural forests), learning fundamental features of plant electrical signals.
AI.result: From the same recorded signals, Bombadil tracks changes in seven physiological indicators of plant stress, including for species and stressors that had no labels during training.
AI.conclusion: A label-free, cross-species and cross-environment foundation model enables scalable, transferable plant stress monitoring from electrophysiological signals.

title: What Language Adds, and at What Cost: Four Controlled Probes of Pathology Vision-Language Models
summary: Vision--language models (VLMs) promise to make computational pathology queryable and able to draft reports, but how much language adds beyond the vision backbone is unclear, because almost every system is evaluated by its developers on test sets of their own choosing. We grade published evidence by how it was produced and test four claims with controlled probes that reuse released checkpoints and public data, varying one input at a time. Report text adds prognostic signal: adding a frozen embedding of the stage-redacted report to a slide embedding raises the pooled C-index by 0.019 for progression-free interval and by 0.016 for overall survival across 1{,}633 TCGA patients, and restoring the stage statement adds nothing. Prompts add no measurable accuracy at inference: with features and pooling fixed, zero-shot classification is statistically indistinguishable from a supervised linear probe for lung and renal cancer subtyping. Slide-level question answering is barely grounded: SlideChat answers 74.82\% of SlideBench-VQA(TCGA) items correctly with the slide and 74.41\% without it, whereas its language backbone alone reaches 43.52\%. Paraphrasing leaves accuracy unchanged but flips 8--23\% of answers. Self-reported gains from agentic navigation and few-shot language priors cannot yet be attributed to language. Language thus adds real but narrow value, and we propose minimum controls that would expose these failure modes in future evaluations.

AI.tldr: A controlled audit of vision-language models in computational pathology finds that language adds real but narrow value: report text improves prognostic prediction, but prompts add no accuracy, and slide-level question answering is barely grounded in the image.
AI.motivation: Almost all VLM pathology systems are evaluated by their own developers on self-chosen test sets, so it is unclear how much language actually adds beyond the vision backbone. The authors want a vendor-neutral, controlled assessment of published claims.
AI.method: They grade published evidence by how it was produced and run controlled probes that reuse released checkpoints and public data, varying one input at a time. Four claims are tested: prognostic value of report text (frozen stage-redacted report embedding added to slide embedding, 1,633 TCGA patients, PFS and OS), value of prompts at inference (zero-shot vs. supervised linear probe for lung/renal subtyping), grounding of slide-level VQA (SlideChat with vs. without slide on SlideBench-VQA(TCGA), plus language-backbone-only baseline), and robustness/attribution (paraphrase stability, self-reported agentic navigation and few-shot priors).
AI.result: Report text adds prognostic signal: +0.019 pooled C-index for progression-free interval and +0.016 for overall survival, while restoring the stage statement adds nothing. Prompts add no measurable inference accuracy (zero-shot statistically indistinguishable from a linear probe). Slide-level VQA is barely grounded: SlideChat scores 74.82% with the slide vs. 74.41% without it, while its language backbone alone reaches 43.52%. Paraphrasing leaves accuracy unchanged but flips 8–23% of answers. Self-reported gains from agentic navigation and few-shot language priors cannot yet be attributed to language.
AI.conclusion: Language adds real but narrow value in computational pathology VLMs, and several reported gains are not attributable to the modality. The authors propose minimum controls that would expose these failure modes in future evaluations.

title: ProteinGeoBench: Frontier Structural-Biology Agents Are Fluent at Lookup but Lost in Geometry
comment: 24 pages, 2 figures, 10 tables. Benchmark and tasks: https://github.com/Protege-AI/ProteinGeoBench
summary: Frontier agents retrieve structural metadata well and compute geometry from coordinates less reliably. We ask how much of a benchmark score reflects that gap and how much reflects the evaluation configuration around the model. We study ProteinGeoBench, a suite of 131 protein-structure tasks, using 4,249 rollouts from four frontier models and 4,486 further trials across 26 models. Three of the four frontier models fall within 0.031 of one another (0.785 to 0.816) with no difference between them resolved, while the fourth scores 0.707 and all three gaps to it exclude zero. Three of the four do better on metadata lookup than on numeric calculation. The fourth is slightly better on numeric. Numeric tasks are 28 of the 131 but half of the twelve tasks that all four models fail. The ranking also depends on the evaluation budget: with one run per task, 23.9% of bootstrap replicates put a different model first. On a selected 15-task slice, removing network access lowers scores more than blocking eight structural-database domains, but the two contrasts were graded in different passes and cannot be cleanly decomposed. Swapping in each model's own command-line agent changes scores by -0.071 to +0.086, a comparison too small to rule out moderate harness effects. Across 26 models, numeric performance rises with non-numeric performance rather than staying flat. The experiments use different task subsets, so they cannot rank model, harness, access and task composition against one another. Evaluations should report results by task family, along with the number of runs, the harness and the access conditions.

AI.tldr: ProteinGeoBench (131 protein-structure tasks) is used to show that benchmark scores conflate model capability with evaluation configuration: top frontier models are near-indistinguishable, small budget/access/harness changes can reshuffle rankings, and results should be reported by task family with run count, harness, and access conditions.
AI.motivation: Frontier agents handle structural metadata well but compute geometry from coordinates less reliably. The authors ask how much of a benchmark score reflects this capability gap versus the evaluation configuration surrounding the model.
AI.method: Analyze ProteinGeoBench, a suite of 131 protein-structure tasks, using 4,249 rollouts from four frontier models plus 4,486 additional trials across 26 models. Compare models, task families (metadata lookup vs. numeric calculation), evaluation budget (bootstrap ranking stability), network/structural-database access, and per-model command-line harnesses.
AI.result: Three of four frontier models lie within 0.031 (0.785–0.816) with no resolved difference; the fourth scores 0.707, with all three gaps excluding zero. Three of four models do better on metadata than numeric tasks; the fourth slightly favors numeric. Numeric tasks are 28 of 131 tasks but half of the twelve tasks all four models fail. With one run per task, 23.9% of bootstrap replicates rank a different model first. On a 15-task slice, removing network access lowers scores more than blocking eight structural-database domains (contrasts graded in different passes, not cleanly separable). Swapping in each model's own CLI agent shifts scores by −0.071 to +0.086, too small to rule out moderate harness effects. Across 26 models, numeric performance rises with non-numeric performance rather than staying flat.
AI.conclusion: The experiments use different task subsets, so model, harness, access, and task composition cannot be ranked against one another. The authors recommend that evaluations report results by task family, along with the number of runs, the harness, and the access conditions.
